grammar.md:
**The first declension.** Feminine nouns ending in -η or -α belong to the first declension. In the singular:

| | ἡ κρήνη | ἡ οἰκία | ἡ θάλαττα |
|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | ἡ κρήν**η** | ἡ οἰκί**α** | ἡ θάλαττ**α** |
| genitive | τῆς κρήν**ης** | τῆς οἰκί**ας** | τῆς θαλάττ**ης** |
| dative | τῇ κρήν**ῃ** | τῇ οἰκί**ᾳ** | τῇ θαλάττ**ῃ** |
| accusative | τὴν κρήν**ην** | τὴν οἰκί**αν** | τὴν θάλαττ**αν** |

Three types: **-η** throughout (κρήνη, κλίνη, σελήνη); **-α** throughout after ε, ι or ρ (οἰκία, ὑδρία, θύρα, ἀγορά, θεά, ἡμέρα); and a short **-α** that switches to -ης / -ῃ in the genitive and dative (θάλαττα). The feminine article is **ἡ, τῆς, τῇ, τήν**; feminine adjectives follow the same pattern: καλή, καλῆς, καλῇ, καλήν but μικρά, μικρᾶς, μικρᾷ, μικράν.

**Three prepositions of place.**

| | case | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **ἐν** | dative | *in*: ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ |
| **εἰς** | accusative | *into, to*: εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν |
| **ἐκ** (ἐξ before a vowel) | genitive | *out of, from*: ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας, ἐξ ἀγορᾶς |

Rest takes the dative, motion towards the accusative, motion from the genitive. The same three words work with masculine nouns too: ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ, εἰς τὸν οἶκον, ἐκ τοῦ οἴκου.

**Third-declension objects** met so far: τὴν πόλιν, τὸν κύνα, τὸν Λύσιν, τὴν Ἐλπίδα. Recognize them; their pattern comes in Unit 3.

culture.title: Women, water and the loom
culture.md: An Athenian citizen's wife like Chrysis ran the household: stores, slaves, children, and above all cloth. Weaving (ὑφαίνειν) on an upright loom was the work that defined a respectable woman, from Penelope onward; the family's clothes, blankets and the robe offered to Athena at the Panathenaea all came off looms like hers. Fetching water was a daily errand, and the fountain house (κρήνη) was one of the few public places where women and girls met and talked. Black-figure hydriai of the sixth century show exactly this scene: women with jars on their heads chatting under the lion-head spouts of a fountain house. Elpis, at nine, would carry a small hydria; the big ones held over twenty litres.
